note: Facts (functions, similar, tools, aliases) come from the site; summary/anatomy/fits/limits are paraphrases; 'ours' is our own characterization. Entries with source.origin='supplement' are not on the site.

charts.name: Arc Diagram
charts.summary: Network links drawn as arcs over a single horizontal line of nodes. Arc thickness shows how often two nodes connect, so a reader scans the arcs for pairs that co-occur and for clusters of linked items.
charts.anatomy: A straight baseline carrying the nodes, semicircular arcs rising above it as links, and arc stroke width encoding link frequency. Node labels sit along the line.
fits: Showing which items co-occur within one sequence
Compact one-dimensional view of a network
Comparing link frequency between pairs of nodes
Spotting clusters of mutual connections
limits: Shows structure less clearly than 2D network diagrams
Too many links make the diagram cluttered
Harder to read as link count grows
Node ordering strongly shapes which patterns appear

ours.scalability: dozens of nodes, ~100 links; order of nodes decides what is visible

charts.name: Proportional Area Chart
charts.summary: Shapes such as squares or circles are sized so their area, not side length, matches each value, giving an at-a-glance sense of relative magnitude without axes. Readers compare how much space each shape occupies, though precise estimates are hard.
charts.anatomy: A set of shapes, usually circles or squares, each scaled by its enclosed area. No axis or gridlines; relative size is the only cue, so labels usually supply exact values.
fits: Quick overview of relative sizes without a scale
Presentation slides where impact outweighs precision
Comparing a few quantities of very different magnitude
Infographics showing shares or counts of items
limits: Sizing by length instead of area exaggerates differences
Values are hard to estimate accurately from area
Better suited to presentation than analytical work
Without labels, exact values remain unclear

discouraged.reason: area is read inaccurately (Stevens ≈0.7); bars compare better; use only for impact with printed values

charts.name: Area Graph
charts.summary: A trend line with the space beneath it filled in, showing how a quantity develops across an interval such as time. Readers judge direction, peaks and overall volume rather than exact values; grouped and stacked variants show several series.
charts.anatomy: Horizontal interval or time axis, vertical value axis, a connecting line through the data points, and a shaded fill from that line down to the baseline. Multiple fills may overlap or stack.
fits: Tracking a quantity's development over time
Emphasising overall volume trends over exact values
Comparing a few series' trajectories side by side
Showing cumulative totals when series are stacked
limits: Exact values are hard to read from the filled shape
Overlapping fills can obscure one another
Stacked layers make lower series harder to compare
Shaded area implies a zero baseline; truncated axes mislead
Not suited to unordered categories

ours.scalability: one or two series; hundreds of time points
ours.chart_types_md_section: Time series / Area / stacked area / streamgraph

charts.name: Bar Chart
charts.summary: Rectangular bars whose lengths are proportional to a value, one bar per discrete category, drawn horizontally or vertically. Readers compare bar lengths against the value scale to see which categories are larger or smaller.
charts.anatomy: A category axis listing the groups, a value axis with a numeric scale, and solid bars starting from a common baseline. Bar length encodes magnitude; bars may be horizontal or vertical.
fits: Comparing values across named categories
Ranking items from largest to smallest
Showing counts for discrete groups
Displaying one measure across several categories
limits: Not for continuous change over an interval
Easily confused with histograms, which bin continuous data
Bars should start at zero to compare fairly
Too many categories crowd the axis and labels

ours.scalability: readable to ~40 bars, hundreds with scrolling; one value per category

charts.name: Box and Whisker Plot
charts.summary: A box covers the middle half of the values with a line inside marking the central value; whiskers stretch toward the extremes and isolated points flag outliers. Readers compare spread, symmetry and skew across groups.
charts.anatomy: A central box spanning the inner quartiles, a median line within it, whiskers extending outward, and individual dots beyond the whisker ends for outliers. Drawn vertically or horizontally.
fits: Comparing distributions across many groups compactly
Spotting outliers in a dataset
Checking whether values are symmetric or skewed
Judging how tightly values cluster
limits: Hides the detailed shape within the box
Less informative than histograms or density plots
Can make multimodal data look ordinary
Whisker rules differ between software packages

ours.scalability: dozens of groups; any n per group

charts.name: Brainstorm
charts.summary: A central topic sits in the middle with main categories radiating outward and smaller branches splitting off them. Readers follow branches from the centre to see how ideas nest and relate; no numeric scale is involved.
charts.anatomy: A central node holding the main topic, labelled primary branches leaving it, and nested sub-branches off those. Layout is radial and free-form rather than axis-based.
fits: Capturing ideas at the start of a project
Organising notes into hierarchical categories
Supporting group brainstorming sessions
Mapping associations between related concepts
Visualising the structure of a topic
limits: Encodes no quantitative values
Becomes cluttered as branches multiply
Relationships are informal and loosely defined
Structure depends on the author's manual choices

discouraged.reason: encodes no data; a concept diagram, not a data visualization

charts.name: Bubble Chart
charts.summary: Labelled circles positioned on two numeric axes, with circle area encoding a third variable and colour often distinguishing categories. Readers compare positions and sizes to spot relationships, correlations and groups.
charts.anatomy: Two numeric axes forming a Cartesian grid, circles whose area represents a value, colour fills for categories, and labels or a legend identifying each bubble. Time may appear as an axis or animation.
fits: Showing three numeric variables in one view
Comparing labelled categories on two measures and size
Revealing correlations across many entities
Animating how entities change over time
limits: Crowded plots become hard to read
Sizing by radius rather than area misleads
Human judgement of circle area is imprecise
Interactivity often needed when bubbles are numerous

ours.scalability: dozens to a few hundred bubbles; size for ≤ 1 order of magnitude

charts.name: Bubble Map
charts.summary: Circles placed over locations on a geographic map, each sized by its area in proportion to a value. Readers compare bubble sizes to see where a quantity concentrates, avoiding the area bias that large shaded regions create.
charts.anatomy: A base map with geographic regions, circles centred on locations, circle area encoding each value, and overlap between neighbouring bubbles. A size key helps readers interpret the scale.
fits: Comparing totals across countries or cities
Avoiding the area bias of shaded regions
Showing point-located values on a map
Revealing where a quantity concentrates geographically
limits: Large bubbles overlap neighbouring bubbles and regions
Overlap can hide smaller values beneath larger ones
Area-based sizes are hard to judge precisely
Needs a size legend to be read accurately

ours.scalability: dozens to hundreds of places; overlap grows with density

charts.name: Bullet Graph
charts.summary: A compact bar showing a main measure, crossed by a short perpendicular marker for a target, and set over shaded bands for qualitative ranges. Readers check whether the bar passes the marker and which band it reaches.
charts.anatomy: A thick central bar for the main value, a perpendicular target line, grey or coloured background bands for performance ranges, and a linear value scale along the length.
fits: Tracking actual performance against a target
Compact KPI displays on dashboards
Showing poor, average and good performance bands
Replacing gauges and meters on dashboards
limits: Works best with no more than about five ranges
Overused bands clutter the display
Shade differences must remain distinguishable
Unfamiliar readers may need explanation

charts.name: Bump chart

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: A line chart of ranks rather than values: each item is a line through its rank at each period, so overtakes appear as crossings. The value itself is not shown.
charts.anatomy: A time axis, a rank axis (1 at the top), one line per item with direct labels at the ends, a highlighted item.
fits: Rank changes over several periods
Replacing an animated bar chart race
Leaderboards over time
limits: Hides magnitudes; a rank change of one may be a large or tiny value change
Many items tangle
Ties need a rule

ours.chart_types_md_section: Time series / Animation / bar chart race

charts.name: Calendar
charts.summary: A grid of day cells arranged into weekday columns and week rows, usually one month per grid, so dates follow chronological order. Readers locate specific days or events and see how time units sequence across the period.
charts.anatomy: Cells each representing one date, column headers for weekdays, rows for weeks, and month or year divisions. Events or colour fills can be placed inside individual cells.
fits: Planning schedules and recurring events
Showing a sequence of dates across months
Displaying daily values across a year
Familiar reference layout for dates
limits: Shows time units rather than continuous magnitudes
Calendar layouts vary across cultures and systems
Long spans require many grids, reducing overview
Dense entries crowd individual cells

ours.scalability: one value per day over months or years
ours.chart_types_md_section: Time series / Calendar heatmap, punch card

charts.name: Candlestick Chart
charts.summary: A financial price chart with one symbol per time period. Each symbol's wide body spans the opening and closing prices, thin wicks reach the period's high and low, and colour indicates whether price rose or fell.
charts.anatomy: Time along the horizontal axis, price on the vertical axis, and candle symbols made of a rectangular real body plus upper and lower shadows. Body colour marks bullish or bearish direction.
fits: Analysing price movement of traded securities
Viewing open, high, low and close per period
Spotting reversal or continuation patterns
Reading daily trading sentiment at a glance
limits: Does not show movement within each period
Easily confused with box plots
Named patterns' predictive value is disputed
Colour conventions differ between markets

charts.name: Chord Diagram
charts.summary: Entities arranged around a circle, joined by arcs or curved ribbons whose width reflects each connection's value. Readers follow the links to see which entities share things in common and how strongly they connect.
charts.anatomy: A ring of labelled segments around the circumference, curved connections between segments, connection width proportional to value, and colour grouping categories.
fits: Comparing similarity within a dataset
Showing flows between groups of entities
Revealing which groups share most in common
Presenting mutual relationships in a circular layout
limits: Clutters quickly when many connections appear
Ribbon ends are hard to trace precisely
Direction of flows can be ambiguous
Exact values need labels or interactivity

charts.name: Choropleth Map
charts.summary: A map whose geographic regions are shaded according to a data value on a colour progression. Readers scan the shading to see regional variation and spatial clusters, though exact figures are difficult to recover from colour.
charts.anatomy: Region boundaries forming the base map, a fill colour or pattern per region, and a colour scale legend linking shades to value ranges. Labels may name the regions.
fits: Showing rates or normalised values across regions
Comparing regional variation on one measure
Spotting spatial clusters or regional gradients
Presenting results by administrative area
limits: Large regions look more important than small ones
Colour makes exact values hard to read
Raw counts mislead unless normalised
Colour scale choice can distort perceived differences

ours.scalability: dozens to thousands of regions; ~5–7 color classes

charts.name: Circle Packing
charts.summary: Nested circles where containment expresses hierarchy: each branch is a circle holding its sub-branches as smaller circles. Circle area can carry an extra quantity. Readers read depth from nesting and size from area.
charts.anatomy: Outer enclosing circles for top-level branches, smaller circles nested inside for sub-branches, circle area encoding a numeric value, and optional colour shades for categories.
fits: Showing nested groups with a size attribute
Revealing hierarchical structure clearly
Displaying file or folder sizes in a tree
Visualising budgets split into nested categories
limits: Wastes space with gaps between circles
Less space-efficient than a treemap
Small nested circles are hard to compare
Area judgements can be imprecise

charts.name: Connected scatterplot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: A scatterplot of two measures where the points of one entity are joined in time order, so the path shows how the two measures co-evolved. Direct year labels on the path replace a time axis.
charts.anatomy: Two quantitative axes, one polyline per entity through its points in time order, arrowheads or labels for direction, a highlighted entity.
fits: Co-evolution of two quantities over time
Trajectories of a few entities
Showing both the relation and the change
limits: Hard to read without direction cues
More than a few entities tangle
Unfamiliar to general readers

ours.chart_types_md_section: Relationships / Connected scatterplot / dumbbell / range plot

charts.name: Connection Map
charts.summary: Points placed on a geographic map, joined by straight or curved lines representing connections between places. Readers trace lines to follow routes or single chains, and dense bundles reveal where links concentrate spatially.
charts.anatomy: A base map with plotted location points, straight or arced lines joining pairs of points, and line styling that may vary by strength or direction.
fits: Showing flight or shipping routes between places
Revealing hubs and concentrated link patterns
Mapping a chain of linked locations
Displaying geographic relationships between many sites
limits: Dense lines create visual clutter quickly
Curved arcs can distort apparent distances
Individual link strength is hard to judge
Overlapping routes hide one another

ours.scalability: dozens to hundreds of links before clutter
ours.chart_types_md_section: Geospatial / Flow / line maps, network maps

charts.name: Table

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: Rows and columns of values with aligned numbers, light row separation and sorted order. The right answer when precision, heterogeneous attributes or a handful of numbers matter more than shape.
charts.anatomy: Header row, one row per item, text left-aligned, numbers right-aligned with equal decimals, optional inline bars or shading, sorted by the key column.
fits: Exact values that will be quoted
Mixed numeric and text attributes
Few values where a chart would be decoration
limits: No overview of shape or trend
Scanning many rows is slow
Unsorted tables hide ranking

ours.scalability: dozens of rows on one screen

charts.name: Density Plot
charts.summary: A smoothed curve over a continuous variable whose height shows how concentrated values are at each point. Readers look for peaks, valleys, skew and the number of modes to understand a distribution's shape.
charts.anatomy: Horizontal axis of the variable's values, vertical density axis, one smoothed line sometimes filled beneath, and peaks marking concentration. Several curves may be overlaid for comparison.
fits: Judging the shape of a numeric distribution
Spotting multiple peaks within data
Comparing smoothed distributions across groups
Avoiding histogram bin-count sensitivity
limits: Smoothing bandwidth can change apparent shape
Smoothing may blur genuine small features
Curve can extend beyond the data's actual range
Densities are not raw counts, confusing lay readers

ours.scalability: a few overlaid groups; n ≥ ~50 per group
ours.chart_types_md_section: Distributions / Violin / strip / beeswarm / ridge / raincloud

charts.name: Donut Chart
charts.summary: A ring-shaped variant of the pie in which arcs stand for parts of a whole. Readers mainly judge arc length rather than slice area, so the hollow centre can hold a headline figure. Suits a few shares; comparing several rings is easier than comparing several pies.
charts.anatomy: A circular ring split into coloured arcs, one per category. Arc length carries the value. The empty centre often holds a total or label, and a legend or direct labels identify each arc.
fits: Showing a few shares of one whole
Highlighting a single headline total in the centre
Tracking how shares shift across several rings
Compact dashboard summaries with few categories
limits: Many small arcs become hard to tell apart
Arc lengths are still tricky to estimate precisely
Misleading when categories do not sum to a whole
Inherits pie criticism about weak comparisons between slices

discouraged.reason: angle is a weak channel; only for ≤5 parts of a whole with simple fractions

charts.name: Dot Map
charts.summary: Identical dots are placed over a geographic base map, each dot marking one item or a fixed number of items. Dense clusters reveal where things concentrate and empty areas show sparseness. It gives an overview of spatial spread rather than exact figures.
charts.anatomy: A base map of a region, uniform point markers, and an optional key stating whether one dot equals one unit or several. Spatial clustering is the main visual signal.
fits: Seeing where events or objects concentrate geographically
Spotting clusters across a region
Giving an overview of spatial distribution
Counting objects where one dot stands for a unit
limits: Exact values are not readable from dot positions
Overlapping dots hide density in crowded areas
Unit size is unclear unless the key is explicit
One-to-many dots make small counts hard to see

ours.scalability: thousands of points; overplotting in dense areas

charts.name: Dot Matrix Chart
charts.summary: A grid of evenly spaced dots, each coloured by category, showing how many items fall into each group. Counting coloured dots gives a quick feel for composition, and several grids can be compared to spot patterns. With one colour it mainly conveys a proportion.
charts.anatomy: A rectangular lattice of identical dots. Colour codes the category, a legend maps colours to groups, and each dot represents one counted unit.
fits: Quick overview of category shares in a dataset
Comparing composition across several groups
Showing discrete counts in an approachable pictogram style
Showing a single share with one colour
Communicating a risk as a frequency, such as 3 in 10
limits: Exact values are hard to read by counting dots
Many colours make categories hard to distinguish
Dot totals need a key to match real quantities
Less useful for very large or continuous data

charts.name: Dot plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: One point per category placed on a quantitative axis, categories sorted by value. Position carries the value, so the axis need not start at zero and small differences stay visible.
charts.anatomy: A category axis with one row per item, a quantitative axis, a dot per item, optional thin stems (lollipop) and value labels.
fits: Comparing values across categories when differences are small
Ranking dozens of items
Showing values whose scale is far from zero
limits: Must be sorted by value or it becomes hard to read
No zero baseline, so readers must check the axis start
Stems add ink without information

ours.scalability: dozens of rows, more with scrolling

charts.name: Dumbbell plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: Each item is a row with two dots joined by a segment, one per state or period; the segment length is the change or gap. Rows are sorted by one of the values or by the gap.
charts.anatomy: A category axis with one row per item, a quantitative axis, two dots of distinct hue per row joined by a line, direct labels.
fits: Gap between two groups per item
Change between two periods with a common scale
Before/after per category
limits: Only two values per item
Sign of the change needs a cue (arrow or color) when dots cross
Many rows need sorting and space

ours.chart_types_md_section: Relationships / Connected scatterplot / dumbbell / range plot

charts.name: Error Bars
charts.summary: A graphical overlay on a Cartesian plot that draws capped lines from a data point to show uncertainty or spread, such as standard error, confidence intervals, or min-max range. Short bars mean values cluster tightly around the plotted point; long bars mean the estimate is less certain.
charts.anatomy: Cap-tipped line segments attached to points or bar edges. They run parallel to a quantitative axis, vertically or horizontally, and may be balanced or unbalanced on each side. The underlying chart supplies the marks.
fits: Showing uncertainty around averages in scientific plots
Adding confidence intervals to bar or line charts
Comparing precision across several estimates
Displaying min and max ranges for each category
limits: Not a standalone chart; needs an underlying plot
Readers may not know which statistic is shown
Symmetric-looking bars can hide skewed data
Mixing standard deviation and standard error causes confusion

charts.name: Flow Chart
charts.summary: A diagram of a process drawn as connected symbols joined by arrows that show the order of steps. Rounded terminators bracket the sequence, rectangles hold actions and diamonds mark decisions with branching paths. Read it by following the arrows from start to finish.
charts.anatomy: Standardised symbols: rounded terminators for start and end, rectangles for steps, diamonds for decisions. Labels sit inside shapes, connecting lines or arrows show direction, and the layout runs horizontally or vertically.
fits: Documenting a multistep procedure or workflow
Explaining an algorithm or system to non-experts
Planning or redesigning an existing process
Showing decision points and alternative branches
limits: Reader must know the symbol conventions
Large processes become tangled and hard to follow
Shows sequence, not timing or durations
Symbol sets vary between tools and organisations

discouraged.reason: a process diagram, not a data visualization; use only to explain a method

charts.name: Flow Map
charts.summary: A geographic map where lines run between places to show the movement of people, goods, or other items, with line thickness scaled to volume. Arrowheads show direction, while plain lines can suggest two-way exchange. Merged or bundled lines reduce clutter.
charts.anatomy: A base map with origin points, flow lines whose width encodes magnitude, optional arrowheads for direction, and bundled lines where routes overlap.
fits: Migration or commuting flows between regions
Trade volumes between countries or ports
Showing where goods or animals travel from and to
Comparing relative size of several routes
limits: Many crossing lines create visual clutter
Line thickness alone makes exact volumes hard to judge
Lines without arrows hide the direction of movement
Bundling can merge distinct routes into one line

ours.chart_types_md_section: Geospatial / Flow / line maps, network maps

charts.name: Gantt Chart
charts.summary: A timeline laid out as a table, where each row is a task and a horizontal bar spans the period it runs. Bar position and length show start, end, duration, and overlap. Dependencies, progress fills, milestones, and a current-date line add detail; it is mainly used to plan and track projects.
charts.anatomy: Task labels down the left, a time scale across the top, horizontal bars placed by start and end, optional arrows for dependencies, partial fills for completion, milestone symbols, and a vertical today-line.
fits: Scheduling and tracking project tasks over time
Seeing which activities run in parallel
Comparing progress against planned durations
Identifying dependencies and the critical path
limits: Becomes unreadable with very many tasks
Does not show cost or resource load by default
Progress fills can be misread without a clear legend
Needs start dates and durations for every task

charts.name: Heatmap (Matrix)
charts.summary: A grid where rows and columns list two sets of categories and each cell's colour encodes a value, categorical or numeric. Shade differences reveal patterns, similarities, and correlations across the matrix. A colour legend is essential for decoding the cells.
charts.anatomy: Row and column labels along the edges, coloured cells at their intersections, a legend mapping colours to categories or a gradient scale, and optionally numbers printed inside cells.
fits: Spotting patterns across two category dimensions
Showing variation across many variables at once
Revealing correlations between variables
Tracking values across time periods and locations
limits: Colour shades are hard to compare precisely
Exact values are hard to extract without cell labels
Meaningless without a legend to decode colours
Colour scales can exaggerate small differences

ours.scalability: hundreds × hundreds of cells; ~10 color levels

charts.name: Histogram
charts.summary: A column chart of one numeric variable's distribution: the horizontal axis is cut into continuous intervals called bins, and each bar's height counts the values in its bin. The overall shape shows where values concentrate, where the extremes lie, and whether gaps or unusual values appear.
charts.anatomy: Touching bars on a continuous horizontal axis, bar height equal to frequency per bin, a vertical count or density axis, and labelled interval ranges. Bin width is a visible design choice.
fits: Checking the shape of a numeric variable
Finding outliers, gaps, or skew in a dataset
Estimating where most observations concentrate
Giving a rough view of a probability distribution
limits: Bin width choice can change the apparent shape
Uneven bin widths mislead unless scaled as density
Not suited to categorical data
Individual values inside each bin are hidden

charts.name: Horizon graph

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: An area chart folded into bands and mirrored for negative values, each band darker the further from the baseline, so many series fit in little vertical space.
charts.anatomy: One narrow row per series, a shared time axis, overlapping bands of increasing darkness, two hues for positive and negative.
fits: Dozens of time series in a small space
Spotting extremes across many series
Monitoring panels
limits: Needs learning
Exact values unreadable
Only for readers who will see it repeatedly

ours.scalability: dozens of series × hundreds of points

charts.name: Illustration Diagram
charts.summary: A picture, which may be a drawing, sketch, wireframe, or photograph, annotated with labels, notes, or a legend. It explains a concept, describes an object or place, or shows how something works or changes. Cutaways and enlargements add depth where needed.
charts.anatomy: A central image carrying the content, callout labels or leader lines, notes or a legend, and optional enlargements or cross-sections. Imagery can be symbolic, pictorial, or realistic.
fits: Explaining how an object or mechanism is built
Describing a place or object with annotations
Teaching a concept through a labelled picture
Showing internal workings with cross-section views
limits: Labels and notes can crowd the image
Accuracy depends on how faithfully the image is drawn
Not data-driven; values are not encoded
Interpretation depends on the annotator's choices

discouraged.reason: an annotated picture, not a data visualization

charts.name: Kagi Chart
charts.summary: A time-independent price chart drawn from vertical lines that reverse direction once price moves past a set reversal amount, with short horizontal joints marking each turn. Thick or green lines indicate rising demand and thin or red lines falling supply; shifts between them are read as trading signals.
charts.anatomy: Vertical line segments, short horizontal shoulders and waists at reversals, line thickness or colour for trend state, a price scale on the right, and date markers on the horizontal axis that are not a true timescale.
fits: Filtering noise from financial price movements
Viewing shifts in supply and demand for an asset
Showing reversal patterns independent of time
Technical analysis of price action
limits: Horizontal date markers are not a real timescale
Reversal amount choice changes the pattern shown
Buy and sell signals are a convention, not guarantees
Time spent between moves is not visible

discouraged.reason: specialist financial idiom; readers need training and the x axis is not time

charts.name: Line Graph
charts.summary: Plots values on a Cartesian grid and joins them with straight segments, usually with time or an ordered sequence on the horizontal axis and a quantity on the vertical. Rising and falling slopes show increases and decreases, so trends and turning points stand out. Several lines can be compared together.
charts.anatomy: A horizontal axis of time or ordered intervals, a vertical quantitative axis, plotted points joined by line segments, values below the baseline for negatives, and separate series distinguished by colour or label.
fits: Showing how a value changes over time
Revealing trends and turning points
Comparing a few series over the same period
Displaying continuous measurements across an interval
limits: Cluttered once more than three or four lines appear
Lines can imply continuity between sparse points
Baseline and axis scaling can exaggerate trends
Small multiples work better for many series

charts.name: Marimekko Chart
charts.summary: A variable-width grid in which both the width and height of each block are percentages. Each column's width shows a category's share, and its stacked segments show subcategory shares, so block area reflects joint share. It reveals how two categorical variables relate, acting as a two-way 100% stacked bar.
charts.anatomy: Columns of differing widths along one axis, stacked segments of varying height within each column, percentage scales on both axes, and category labels on the axes or inside blocks.
fits: Comparing market share across two categorical dimensions
Showing how segments divide within each column
General overview of category relationships
Contribution to totals by brand and region
limits: Hard to read with many segments
Segments lack a common baseline, complicating comparisons
Narrow columns make labels and values cramped
Best for overview rather than precise comparison

discouraged.reason: areas without a common baseline; use for an overview of two shares only

charts.name: Multi-set Bar Chart
charts.summary: A bar chart in which two or more series share one value axis and sit side by side inside parent-category groups. Bar length gives discrete values and colour tells series apart. It suits comparing matching subcategories across groups, comparing mini histograms, or showing change over time within clusters.
charts.anatomy: Clusters of adjacent bars on a common value axis, one colour per series, group labels beneath each cluster, a legend naming the series, and visible gaps separating the groups.
fits: Comparing subcategories across parent categories
Showing several series side by side
Comparing mini histograms across groups
Tracking yearly change within each cluster
limits: Harder to read as bars per group increase
Needs a legend when many colours are used
Keep the number of bars per group small
Crowded when there are many groups

charts.name: Network Diagram
charts.summary: Nodes drawn as dots or icons are joined by link lines that show which entities connect and how. Node size or line weight can encode extra values, and small arrows can mark one-way or two-way ties. Readers look for clusters, connection density, and overall layout structure.
charts.anatomy: Nodes as circles or icons, links as lines between them, optional arrowheads for direction, variable node sizes or stroke widths for extra values, and the spatial arrangement that reveals clusters.
fits: Mapping relationships among people or organisations
Spotting clusters and densely linked groups
Showing directed influence between entities
Exploring the structure of connected systems
limits: Becomes a hairball with many nodes
Layout algorithm choice shapes apparent clustering
Limited capacity for detailed data per node
Exact paths are hard to follow in dense networks

ours.scalability: dozens to a few hundred nodes; hairball beyond

charts.name: Nightingale Rose Chart
charts.summary: Segments of a circle, each assigned to a category or time interval, extend outward by different distances from a central point; the radial distance encodes the value. Readers compare how far each wedge reaches from the center, usually along the rings used as a scale.
charts.anatomy: Polar grid of concentric rings acting as the value scale, equal-angle wedges per category, and wedge length from the centre as the encoded mark. Readers should judge radius rather than wedge area.
fits: Showing category values across a full cycle or set of intervals
Presentational displays of values for a general audience
Historical or stylised reports where visual impact matters
Proportions or values over time in a radial layout
limits: Outer wedges look larger, exaggerating value increases
Wedge area perception makes precise comparisons difficult
Readers must decode a polar grid, which takes effort
Radial scale is harder to read than a straight axis

discouraged.reason: radius/area encoding exaggerates outer values; a bar or line is more accurate

charts.name: Non-ribbon Chord Diagram
charts.summary: Nodes arranged around a circle are joined by connector lines, with no filled bands between them. Readers trace which entities link to which, focusing on the web of connections rather than the size of each link.
charts.anatomy: Nodes placed around a ring, with lines drawn across the interior between linked nodes. No ribbon fills appear; the lines alone carry the connections.
fits: Revealing which entities in a network connect to each other
Emphasising the overall web of connections in the data
Cleaner alternative when ribbon fills would clutter the view
Showing relationships between a modest set of categories
limits: Link thickness or flow size is not conveyed without ribbons
Dense networks make individual connection lines hard to follow
Unsuited where exact link quantities must be read
Circular layout order strongly affects how readable it is

charts.name: Open-High-Low-Close Chart
charts.summary: Each time period is drawn as a vertical bar spanning the highest to lowest price, with small ticks on the left and right for opening and closing values. Readers judge each period's sentiment and look for recurring formations across the timeline.
charts.anatomy: Vertical price scale and horizontal time axis. Each mark has a central line for the high-low span, a left tick for the open, a right tick for the close, with hue marking rising or falling periods.
fits: Tracking daily price movements of stocks or currencies
Spotting trend reversals through repeated price formations
Showing the price range and open-to-close change per period
Comparing market sentiment across consecutive trading periods
limits: Does not show trading volume unless paired with another chart
Small ticks are hard to read when the series is dense
Colour coding for bullish or bearish needs an explicit key
Past price patterns do not reliably predict future moves

charts.name: Parallel Coordinates Plot
charts.summary: Many variables are drawn as vertical axes side by side, and each record becomes a line crossing every axis at its value. Readers follow individual lines or bundles to compare items across attributes and to spot correlations between neighbouring axes.
charts.anatomy: Vertical axes, one per variable, stand side by side and may share or differ in scale. Polylines connect a record's value on every axis. Axis order affects how easily adjacent relationships are read.
fits: Comparing many products sharing the same attribute set
Exploring multivariate numeric data for correlations
Comparing specs such as cars or computers across models
Interactive exploration where highlighting isolates lines of interest
limits: Dense datasets become illegible without interactive filtering
Reordering axes changes which patterns appear obvious
Non-adjacent axes are harder to relate than neighbouring ones
Mixed units need per-axis scales or normalisation to compare

ours.scalability: ≤ ~12 axes; hundreds of items, thousands with opacity

charts.name: Parallel Sets
charts.summary: Categorical dimensions appear as stacked vertical bands, with flows drawn between them as ribbons whose widths reflect each category's share. Readers follow a ribbon from one dimension to the next to see how groups split and recombine, and can colour flows to compare categories.
charts.anatomy: Vertical bands, one per categorical dimension, split into labelled segments. Ribbons link segments across adjacent bands, and their width tracks each category's share.
fits: Showing how categorical groups distribute across several attributes
Following respondents through multiple classification questions
Comparing category composition between linked dimensions
Interactive exploration of categorical data in analysis
Flows without direction, where arrows would imply a sequence
limits: Often confused with Sankey and alluvial diagrams
No arrows, so direction of movement is not implied
Many ribbons crossing bands become tangled and hard to trace
Ribbon widths judged by eye, so exact values need labels

charts.name: Pictogram Chart
charts.summary: Rows or columns of repeated icons stand for counts across a small set of discrete categories, each icon representing one unit or a fixed multiple of one. Readers count icons and compare row or column lengths side by side.
charts.anatomy: Rows or columns of identical icons, one row per category. A key states the value each icon stands for. Partial icons are best avoided, since they confuse the count.
fits: Small sets of discrete counts for a general audience
Audiences where language, culture or education varies
Countable subjects such as people, cars or animals
Presentations where icons add visual engagement
limits: Large data sets make icons too numerous to count
Partial icons confuse what each symbol represents
Unit value must be stated clearly on the chart
Icons may not map cleanly onto abstract categories

charts.name: Pie Chart
charts.summary: A circle is split into wedges whose arc lengths or angles represent each category's share of the total, which equals the full circle. Readers estimate each slice's proportion, and judging one slice against the whole is more dependable than comparing slices across several pies.
charts.anatomy: Circle divided into wedges, each wedge a category; the full circle equals the total. A legend or direct labels identify slices, and arc length or angle encodes the proportion.
fits: Showing a few categories as shares of one total
Quick proportional overview for presentations or offices
Highlighting one segment against the whole
Two to five categories with clearly different sizes
limits: Too many slices become thin and unreadable
Comparing slices across several pies is difficult
Uses more space than a 100% stacked bar chart
Usually needs a legend, adding visual overhead

discouraged.reason: angle is a weak channel; only for ≤5 parts of a whole with simple fractions; sorted bars compare better

charts.name: Point & Figure Chart
charts.summary: Stacked Xs and Os form columns that plot filtered price moves: X marks rising prices, O marks falling ones, and a new column begins only after a set reversal. Horizontal spacing is not elapsed time; readers look for breakouts and support or resistance levels.
charts.anatomy: Vertical value scale for price. Each column holds only X or only O symbols, and columns advance left to right. Occasional month markers use 1-9 for January to September and A, B, C for October to December.
fits: Filtering minor price noise to reveal supply-demand shifts
Spotting support, resistance and trend lines in prices
Analysing asset prices without volume or elapsed-time scaling
Studying breakout patterns in securities or commodities
limits: Ignores trading volume and does not plot elapsed time
Box size and reversal amount strongly change the appearance
Date markers on the x-axis are not a true timescale
Results depend on the chosen price basis and settings

discouraged.reason: specialist financial idiom without a time axis

charts.name: Population Pyramid
charts.summary: Two back-to-back sets of horizontal bars, one for each sex, extend from a central axis to show population counts within each age band. Readers judge the overall silhouette to infer demographic structure and compare the two sexes within each age group.
charts.anatomy: Central vertical axis listing age groups; horizontal bars extend left and right, one side per sex; horizontal axis carries population counts. Bar lengths on the two sides reveal sex balance.
fits: Showing the age and sex makeup of a national population
Comparing demographic structure across countries or regions
Tracking population change across successive census years
Teaching ageing and fertility trends in sociology or ecology
limits: Shape-based readings of future trends are speculative
Only age and sex appear, so other factors stay hidden
Mirrored bars make precise cross-side comparison harder
Raw counts need normalising to compare different-sized populations

charts.name: Radar Chart
charts.summary: Several variables radiate from a central point, each on its own equally spaced axis, and one series' values join into a closed polygon. Readers compare overall profile shape and spot which variables score high or low, mostly for a few series at a time.
charts.anatomy: Spokes radiate from a centre, one per variable, all sharing one scale. Grid webs or rings guide the eye. Each series appears as a polygon joining its values on the spokes.
fits: Comparing performance profiles across several attributes
Showing which variables run high or low for one item
Spotting outliers among a handful of variables
Visualising player or athlete statistics side by side
limits: Overlapping polygons become cluttered as series increase
Filled shapes hide series drawn beneath them
Many spokes overwhelm readers
Values are hard to compare directly across axes

discouraged.reason: polygon shape depends on arbitrary axis order; bars or parallel coordinates compare better

charts.name: Radial Bar Chart
charts.summary: Bars laid out on a circular frame extend outward from a shared centre, each at its own radius. Readers compare bar extents around the ring, remembering that outer bars can look longer even at equal values.
charts.anatomy: Bars radiate from a central origin, each placed at its own radius; the reader must account for radius when judging length.
fits: Aesthetic circular displays where looks matter more than precision
Ranking a small set of categories in a radial layout
Circular dashboards or infographics with a ring theme
Decorative charts meant to stand out on a page
limits: Bar lengths mislead, since outer bars appear longer
Linear bar charts are better for accurate comparison
Mainly justified by aesthetics rather than analysis

discouraged.reason: outer bars are longer for the same value: the geometry lies; use a bar chart

charts.name: Radial Column Chart
charts.summary: Columns are plotted on a polar grid, with concentric rings forming the value scale and radial spokes separating categories. Each column rises outward from the centre by its value, so readers match each column to its spoke and read height against the rings.
charts.anatomy: Rings mark the value scale; radial dividers separate categories; column bars extend outward from the centre. Placing zero on an outer ring lets inner rings hold negatives.
fits: Categories arranged around a circle with clear value rings
Showing values that include negatives on one scale
Compact circular comparisons of several categories
Star-shaped displays for presentations or dashboards
limits: Reading column height against curved rings is harder
Circular scales make precise value reading harder
Negative-value layouts need careful ring labelling
Ring spacing must be labelled to be interpreted

discouraged.reason: curved scale reads worse than a straight bar chart; cyclic data only

charts.name: Ridge plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: Stacked, slightly overlapping density curves, one per group or period, sharing one value axis, so shifts in location and shape across the groups read as a landscape.
charts.anatomy: A shared quantitative axis, one row per group in a meaningful order, filled density curves that may overlap the row above, direct row labels.
fits: How a distribution shifts across many periods or groups
Dozens of distributions in one panel
Ordered groups (months, years, latitude bands)
limits: No exact values
Overlap hides the tails of the row behind
Needs an order; unordered groups are better as violins

ours.chart_types_md_section: Distributions / Violin / strip / beeswarm / ridge / raincloud

charts.name: Sankey Diagram
charts.summary: Bands whose thickness matches quantity trace energy, material, money or any process flow, branching or merging at each stage. Readers follow the widest paths to see where most of the flow goes, with colour often marking categories or stages.
charts.anatomy: Nodes or stages joined by flow bands, each band's width proportional to its quantity. Bands split and combine at nodes, with hue distinguishing categories or a change of state.
fits: Energy transfer or material flows through a system
Money moving through budgets, revenues or costs
Multi-stage processes with losses or transfers between stages
Comparing alternative routes through a process
limits: Easily mistaken for alluvial diagrams or parallel sets
Crossing bands in dense diagrams become hard to trace
Node ordering strongly affects how readable the flows are
Band widths judged by eye, so exact values need labels

charts.name: Scatterplot
charts.summary: Each record appears as a point placed by two numeric variables along horizontal and vertical axes. Readers look at how the cloud rises, falls, bends or stays flat to judge correlation direction, shape, strength and any outliers.
charts.anatomy: Two numeric axes meeting at an origin; each point is one paired observation. An optional trend line overlays the cloud, and isolated points far from the cluster are outliers.
fits: Testing whether two numeric variables move together
Spotting outliers in paired measurements
Estimating values with a fitted trend line
Checking non-linear shapes such as U-shaped relationships
Exploring relationships before building predictive models
limits: Correlation does not imply causation; hidden variables may drive results
Overlapping points hide density when many observations exist
Trend lines can suggest precision the data lacks
Needs paired numerical data for both axes

charts.name: Slope chart

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: Two vertical axes for two moments; each item is a line joining its value at each moment. Slope direction and steepness show change; crossing lines show rank changes.
charts.anatomy: Two labelled vertical axes, one line per item with direct labels at both ends, and a highlighted line for the item of interest.
fits: Change of many items between two periods
Rank changes between two moments
Before/after comparisons
limits: Only two time points
Dozens of lines need a highlight-and-grey design
Needs a wide enough panel to read slopes

charts.name: Small multiples

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: The same chart repeated once per category in a grid with shared axes, so the reader compares shapes across panels instead of untangling overlaid series.
charts.anatomy: A grid of equally sized panels, one per category, identical axes and scales, a shared legend, panel titles, logical panel order.
fits: Many series over time
Comparing a pattern across groups
Replacing animation with side-by-side frames
limits: Panels get small when there are many categories
Shared scales flatten small series; independent scales break comparison
Needs space

charts.name: Span Chart
charts.summary: Each category gets a bar that floats between its lowest and highest value, so readers compare where ranges start and stop and how wide they are across groups.
charts.anatomy: A category axis, a value axis, and one floating bar per category whose bottom and top edges mark the minimum and maximum. Bar length shows the spread.
fits: Comparing value ranges across several categories
Showing minimum and maximum values per group
Displaying durations of events on a timeline
Visualising low-to-high spreads such as price or temperature
limits: Shows only the extremes, not averages or distribution
Gives no information between minimum and maximum values

ours.chart_types_md_section: Relationships / Connected scatterplot / dumbbell / range plot

charts.name: Spiral Plot
charts.summary: Time-based values are drawn along a path that winds outward from a central start point, so repeating cycles appear as loops lined up around the spiral. Colour can mark each period.
charts.anatomy: A start point at the centre, a continuous outward-winding path, and marks (bars, lines or dots) placed along that path, with optional colour bands per period.
fits: Very large time series spanning long periods
Revealing periodic or seasonal patterns
Comparing successive cycles using colour per period
Showing daily, monthly or yearly rhythms in one view
limits: Reading exact values is harder than on straight axes
Less familiar to general audiences, so needs explaining
Outer loops are longer, which distorts length comparison

discouraged.reason: unfamiliar and outer loops distort lengths; a calendar heatmap shows cycles with less learning

charts.name: Stacked Area Graph
charts.summary: Several series are layered so each one rests on the top edge of the previous; the top boundary is the running total. Readers compare band thickness and overall height over time.
charts.anatomy: A time axis along the bottom, a value axis rising from zero, coloured bands stacked upward with a boundary line each, and a legend naming each series.
fits: Showing how several parts add up over time
Tracking each category's contribution across periods
Displaying overall totals alongside component trends
Comparing multiple variables changing in the same period
limits: Values must be non-negative, since areas convey whole quantities
Middle bands are hard to read off a shifting baseline
Only the bottom series sits on a common baseline

ours.chart_types_md_section: Time series / Area / stacked area / streamgraph

charts.name: Stacked Bar Graph
charts.summary: Bars are divided into stacked segments, so each bar's total length shows the whole and each segment shows a part. The 100% variant rescales bars so segments read as shares.
charts.anatomy: Categories along one axis, bars subdivided into coloured segments, a value axis (raw or 0-100%), and a legend matching colours to subcategories.
fits: Showing totals split into subcategories per group
Comparing overall totals between a few groups
Part-of-a-whole shares across categories in the 100% version
Seeing how composition differs between bars
limits: Gets harder to read as the number of segments rises
Segments lack a common baseline, so middle ones are hard to compare
The 100% version hides absolute totals

charts.name: Stem and Leaf Plot
charts.summary: Each value is split into a stem (leading digits) and a leaf (final digit); leaves hang beside their stems in ascending order, so the shape of the data shows while raw values stay visible.
charts.anatomy: A vertical column of stem values in ascending order, with each row's leaves listed sideways from it. Back-to-back layouts place two datasets on either side of the stems.
fits: Small datasets where raw values should stay visible
Spotting outliers and the mode quickly
Comparing two small datasets back to back
Reference listings such as transport schedules
limits: Too few values make the plot pointless
Too many values clutter the display and reduce readability
Practical size limit on the datasets it can handle

charts.name: Stream Graph
charts.summary: Stacked bands wiggle around a moving central baseline, forming a flowing, river-like shape. Band thickness along the time axis shows each category's value, favouring overall trends over exact figures.
charts.anatomy: A horizontal time axis through the middle, coloured organic bands stacked around a shifting centre, and a colour legend. No value axis is drawn.
fits: Overviewing many categories across long periods
Spotting seasonal peaks and recurring patterns
Showing volatility across a large group of assets
Engaging presentation or interactive pieces for general audiences
limits: Small categories get drowned out by large ones
No value axis, so exact values cannot be read
Cluttered with large datasets, which hurts legibility
Works best as an interactive piece rather than static

ours.scalability: hundreds of time steps; dozens of categories
ours.chart_types_md_section: Time series / Area / stacked area / streamgraph

charts.name: Strip plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Wilke 2019 / Few 2004

charts.summary: Every observation is drawn at its true position on a quantitative axis, one strip per group, as thin ticks or translucent or hollow points, so darker stretches mean more values. The reader sees the raw spread, gaps and outliers, usually with a median mark overlaid.
charts.anatomy: A category axis with one strip per group, a quantitative axis, one tick or translucent point per observation at its exact value, optional median marker and labelled interval.
fits: Comparing groups on a measured variable with the raw data visible
Small to medium n per group
Replacing bars of means
A raw-data layer under a density or summary
limits: Thousands of points per group overplot; switch to violin or density
Ties hide behind each other without opacity or hollow marks
Random jitter changes on every render; seed it or use a beeswarm
Any sideways offset adds no information

ours.chart_types_md_section: Distributions / Violin / strip / beeswarm / ridge / raincloud

charts.name: Sunburst Diagram
charts.summary: Concentric rings show levels of a hierarchy, with the root at the centre and child categories sliced outward; each slice's angle is equal or proportional to a value. Readers trace paths from the centre outward.
charts.anatomy: A central root circle, concentric rings for each hierarchy level, wedge slices nested under their parent slices, and colour grouping related categories.
fits: Showing nested hierarchies across a few levels
Part-to-whole breakdowns with multiple levels
Highlighting groupings with colour
Displaying multi-level proportions in a compact form
limits: Angles on outer rings are hard to compare
Outer levels get cramped and hard to label
Deep hierarchies quickly become cluttered

charts.name: Tally Chart
charts.summary: Each occurrence of a category adds one mark in its row or column, and totals are counted at the end. The finished tally resembles a histogram and shows the frequency of each category.
charts.anatomy: Category labels down one side, columns or rows of tally marks beside them, and a total column counted at the end.
fits: Recording frequencies while counting live
Quick manual counts with no software
Building a frequency table before drawing a histogram
Simple observations or surveys of categories
limits: Manual counting makes errors likely in large datasets
Only suits counting discrete categories or intervals
Result is a table of counts rather than a visual chart

discouraged.reason: a counting aid; a sorted bar chart or a table serves the reader better

charts.name: Timeline
charts.summary: Events are placed in chronological order along a line, either on a true time scale where spacing reflects real intervals or simply in sequence. Readers use position and spacing to judge timing.
charts.anatomy: A linear axis or line, markers or labels at event positions, optional date scale ticks, and descriptive text or cards attached to each event.
fits: Narrating historical or project events in order
Showing gaps and intervals between events on a scale
Pairing with bars to show event durations
Revealing when events cluster or spread out
limits: Unscaled timelines hide real time intervals
Crowded events overlap and become hard to read
Shows event timing, not quantities

charts.name: Timetable
charts.summary: A grid of scheduled events, tasks or departures, ordered by time or name so readers can look up an entry quickly. Readers locate a row and column to find a specific time.
charts.anatomy: Rows and columns forming a grid, headers for times or categories, entries in the cells, and a consistent sort order running through the table.
fits: Transport arrival and departure schedules
Organising scheduled tasks or actions
Quick reference lists sorted by time or name
limits: Dense grids are hard to scan at a glance
Does not visually show durations or overlaps
Static tables must be updated when schedules change

charts.name: Tree Diagram
charts.summary: A branching structure with a root at the top, nodes linked by branches, and leaf nodes at the ends; it shows parent-child relationships and levels of hierarchy. Readers follow branches to find ancestors or descendants.
charts.anatomy: A root node, internal nodes, connecting branch lines between parents and children, and leaf end-nodes that have no children.
fits: Family trees and descent relationships
Biological classification and taxonomy
Evolutionary history of species
Organisational and management reporting structures
limits: Large trees become wide and hard to navigate
Shows structure and relationships, not quantities

ours.scalability: dozens to a few hundred nodes; depth ≤ 6

charts.name: Treemap
charts.summary: Nested rectangles where each category's area is proportional to its value, with subcategories sitting inside their parent. Readers compare rectangle sizes to judge shares of the total.
charts.anatomy: Outer rectangles for top-level groups, smaller rectangles nested inside for subcategories, area encoding the value, and colour for groups or variables.
fits: Showing shares of a total across many categories
Compact display of a large hierarchy
Overviewing file or directory sizes
Comparing proportions between categories by area
limits: Hierarchy levels are less clear than in tree or sunburst charts
Tiling algorithm changes rectangle shapes and ordering
Hard to compare very similar or thin rectangles

ours.scalability: hundreds to thousands of leaves; depth ≤ 3

charts.name: Venn Diagram
charts.summary: Overlapping shapes, usually circles, each stand for a set; items in an overlap belong to every set covering that region. Readers check which regions hold shared membership.
charts.anatomy: Circles representing sets, overlapping intersection zones where shared items sit, and labels naming each set.
fits: Showing shared membership between two or three groups
Explaining logical intersections and set relationships
Comparing overlap between categories or concepts
limits: Geometry gets complex beyond three or four sets
Circle overlap areas do not encode exact quantities
Hard to draw cleanly when many sets are involved

charts.name: Violin Plot
charts.summary: Mirrored density curves form a shape around a central box-like marker; the width at each height shows how many values fall there. Readers read shape for modes and skew, and median and spread from the centre.
charts.anatomy: A symmetric density outline mirrored around a vertical axis, a white median dot, a thick central bar for the interquartile range, and a thin line for min and max values.
fits: Comparing distribution shapes across several groups
Spotting bimodal or multimodal distributions
Showing median and spread together in one view
limits: Visually noisier than a plain box plot
Marker can be clipped at the ends of the thin line
Density smoothing can hide or invent features in small samples

ours.chart_types_md_section: Distributions / Violin / strip / beeswarm / ridge / raincloud

charts.name: Word Cloud
charts.summary: Words are sized by how often they occur in a text, then arranged into a cluster; colour is usually decorative. The eye goes to the largest words as the most frequent terms.
charts.anatomy: Words as text labels, font size encoding frequency or an attached value, arrangement in a cluster or shape, and optional colour categories.
fits: Quick overview of frequent keywords or tags
Website or blog tag usage display
Rough comparison of two bodies of text
Decorative summary of a topic or text
limits: Long words look bigger than short ones
Letter shapes with ascenders receive extra attention
Poor for analytical accuracy; mostly aesthetic

discouraged.reason: area depends on word length; a sorted bar chart of top terms compares better

charts.name: Dendrogram

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014

charts.summary: A tree produced by hierarchical clustering. Every leaf sits on the same baseline and two branches join at a height equal to the distance at which their clusters merge, so the reader sees which items group early (similar) and which only join near the top.
charts.anatomy: Leaves aligned on one level with labels, right-angled branches, a quantitative merge-distance axis, optional cut line that defines the clusters.
fits: Showing how items group at successive similarity levels
Choosing a number of clusters by cutting at a height
Ordering the rows or columns of a heatmap
Comparing two clusterings side by side
limits: Leaf order is partly arbitrary: branches can flip freely
Neighbouring leaves are not necessarily similar
Result depends on the distance and linkage chosen; state them
Hundreds of leaves make labels unreadable

ours.scalability: up to a few hundred leaves; labels readable to ~60

charts.name: Indented tree

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014

charts.summary: A hierarchy written as a vertical list, one node per line, with horizontal indentation showing depth. Labels all start on a readable line, so scanning for a name is fast, and columns of attributes can sit beside each row.
charts.anatomy: One text row per node, indentation steps for depth, optional expand/collapse markers and guide lines, optional aligned attribute columns or inline bars.
fits: Looking up a node by name in a deep hierarchy
Showing attributes of every node in aligned columns
Hierarchies with long labels
Interactive drill-down by expanding branches
limits: Uses one line per node, so tall trees scroll far
Overall shape and breadth of the tree are hard to see
Siblings far apart vertically are hard to relate
Poor at showing several scales at once

ours.scalability: thousands of nodes with collapsing; ~50 rows visible at once

charts.name: Icicle plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Kruskal & Landwehr 1983

charts.summary: A space-filling hierarchy in rectangular coordinates: each level is a band, each node a rectangle placed directly under its parent, and the node's length along the band is proportional to its value. Depth and size are read on two separate straight axes.
charts.anatomy: Stacked bands, one per level; rectangles whose length encodes value; children aligned beneath their parent; labels inside the rectangles; root band spanning the full extent.
fits: Seeing structure and size together with aligned lengths
Comparing sizes within one level along a common axis
Profiling call stacks or nested costs (flame graph)
Hierarchies of moderate depth with labelled nodes
limits: Deep levels shrink to slivers too thin to label
Every level costs a full band of space
Sizes in different levels are not on a common baseline
Sibling order must be meaningful or sorted by size

charts.name: Adjacency matrix

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Ghoniem et al. 2005 / Behrisch et al. 2016 / Munzner 2014

charts.summary: A network drawn as a square grid: every node is both a row and a column and a filled cell marks a link between the pair, shaded by weight. Nothing crosses, so dense graphs stay legible; clusters appear as blocks once rows and columns are reordered.
charts.anatomy: The same node list on rows and columns, one cell per node pair, cell shade for link weight, a diagonal for self-links, optional cluster brackets.
fits: Dense networks where a node-link drawing becomes a hairball
Finding clusters, cliques and hubs as blocks and stripes
Checking whether a specific pair is linked
Showing weighted or directed links without clutter
limits: The ordering decides what is visible; a poor order hides everything
Following a path over several hops is hard
Space grows with the square of the node count
Unfamiliar to general readers; needs a reading guide
Sparse graphs waste most of the grid

ours.scalability: up to ~1,000 nodes with one pixel per cell; labels readable to ~100

charts.name: UpSet plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Lex et al. 2014

charts.summary: Bars give the size of every combination of sets, and a dot matrix under the bars shows which sets each combination contains. Bar length makes intersection sizes exactly comparable, and the layout keeps working well past the three sets a Venn diagram can hold.
charts.anatomy: Sorted bars of intersection size, a matrix with one row per set and filled connected dots marking membership, side bars for total set sizes.
fits: Four or more overlapping sets
Ranking the largest or emptiest combinations
Exact comparison of intersection sizes
Filtering combinations by degree or minimum size
limits: Readers must learn the matrix before the bars make sense
Combinations double with every added set; truncate and say so
Containment is less intuitive than overlapping circles
Sort order changes the story; state it

ours.scalability: up to ~20 sets; show the top ~40 combinations

charts.name: Sparkline

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Tufte 2006

charts.summary: A line chart shrunk to the size of a word and stripped of axes, placed inside a table cell, a dashboard tile or a sentence. It shows the shape of recent history next to the current number, not exact values.
charts.anatomy: A short unframed line, optional dot on the last or extreme point, optional shaded normal band, the current value printed beside it.
fits: Adding trend context to a number in a table
Dozens of series scanned row by row
Dashboards with little room per indicator
Showing shape when exact values are printed elsewhere
limits: No axis: magnitudes cannot be read or compared across rows
Each row usually has its own scale; say so
Aspect ratio exaggerates or flattens slopes
Too small for annotation or more than one series

charts.name: Raincloud plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Allen et al. 2019 / Correll 2023

charts.summary: A combined view of one distribution per group: a half density for shape, the individual values for sample size and gaps, and a summary mark for the centre. Each part should compensate for what another part hides, otherwise it only adds ink.
charts.anatomy: A half density curve, a strip of ticks or points at their true values beneath it, a median marker with a labelled quantile interval, one row per group.
fits: Reporting group differences with raw data and summary together
Small to medium samples where shape and n both matter
Readers who need a summary but must check the data
Replacing bars of means in scientific figures
limits: Density plus random jitter plus box plot repeats the same weaknesses
Smoothing invents mass for discrete or bounded data
Three layers per group need generous row height
The interval shown must be named
Bandwidth choice changes the apparent shape

ours.scalability: ≤ ~10 groups; tens to a few thousand points per group
ours.chart_types_md_section: Distributions / Violin / strip / beeswarm / ridge / raincloud

charts.name: Beeswarm plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Wilke 2019 / Eklund 2012 (beeswarm package)

charts.summary: Every observation is a dot on a quantitative axis, pushed sideways just far enough that no two dots overlap. The packing is deterministic and the swarm widens where values are frequent, so it shows each point and the rough shape at once.
charts.anatomy: One swarm per group along a quantitative axis, non-overlapping dots, sideways spread without meaning, optional median marker.
fits: Small to medium samples where every point should be visible
Showing ties and clusters that a strip would overplot
Reproducible alternative to random jitter
Colouring individual points by a second attribute
limits: Packing shifts dots slightly off their true value
Swarm width depends on dot size, not only on density
Breaks down beyond a few hundred points per group
Sideways position carries no data
Layout algorithms differ between tools

ours.chart_types_md_section: Distributions / Violin / strip / beeswarm / ridge / raincloud

charts.name: Wilkinson dot plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Wilkinson 1999

charts.summary: Observations are binned along the axis and drawn as dots stacked in columns, one dot per observation. It reads like a histogram whose bars can be counted, which suits small samples and audiences who prefer counts to densities.
charts.anatomy: A quantitative axis, columns of equally sized dots stacked from a baseline, one dot per observation, bin width equal to dot diameter.
fits: Small samples where each observation should be countable
Teaching distributions without a density scale
Discrete or rounded measurements
Showing gaps and repeated values honestly
limits: Binning moves values to the column position
Bin width and dot size are tied; changing one changes the picture
Stacks outgrow the plot beyond a few hundred points
Easily confused with a Cleveland dot plot of categories

charts.name: Quantile dot plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Kay et al. 2016 / Fernandes et al. 2018

charts.summary: A predictive or posterior distribution drawn as a few dozen stacked dots, each standing for an equal slice of probability. Readers count dots on either side of a threshold to get a chance such as 3 in 20, without reading a density or an interval.
charts.anatomy: A quantitative axis, 20 to 100 equal dots stacked in columns, an optional threshold line, a caption stating what one dot is worth.
fits: Forecasts for lay readers who must judge a risk
Decisions against a threshold, such as arriving late
Skewed or multimodal predictive distributions
Replacing an interval that readers take as a hard range
limits: Mistaken for raw observations when shown beside data dots
The dot count sets the resolution of probabilities
Needs a sentence explaining the value of one dot
Takes more space than an interval per estimate

charts.name: Gradient interval plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Padilla, Kay & Hullman 2021 / Correll & Gleicher 2014

charts.summary: An estimate drawn with its uncertainty as nested or fading bands: a central line or point, darker ink where values are more probable, lighter towards the tails. Along time it becomes a fan that widens with the forecast horizon.
charts.anatomy: A central estimate line or point, one or more shaded bands for named probability levels, fading opacity outward, a legend stating each level.
fits: Forecasts whose uncertainty grows over time
Estimates per category with a stated interval
Avoiding the false cliff of a single hard-edged interval
Expert readers comparing estimates and their precision
limits: Band edges get read as limits the value cannot cross
On maps or paths the band looks like a physical area
Probability levels must be labelled or the bands mean nothing
Opacity steps are hard to compare precisely
Overlapping bands of several series blend together

ours.scalability: 1–4 series over time, or dozens of estimates as rows; ≤ 3–4 bands

charts.name: Ensemble plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Padilla, Kay & Hullman 2021 / Whitaker et al. 2013

charts.summary: One line or path per model run, simulation or posterior draw, overlaid in a thin translucent stroke. Agreement shows as a tight bundle and uncertainty as spread; a contour boxplot summarises the same members into a median path and bands.
charts.anatomy: Many thin semi-transparent lines sharing both axes, an optional highlighted mean or median member, a note on how many members and from which run.
fits: Showing forecast spread without assuming a distribution shape
Revealing distinct scenarios that a band would average away
Trajectories or paths from a simulation ensemble
Expert readers who know the models behind the members
limits: Members from different models or dates are not comparable
Line density reflects member count, not only probability
Dozens of lines tangle; individual members cannot be followed
One odd member attracts more attention than it deserves
Readers may take each line as an equally likely outcome

charts.name: Hypothetical outcome plot

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Hullman, Resnick & Adar 2015 / Kale et al. 2019

charts.summary: An animation in which each frame is one plausible outcome drawn from the distribution, shown with the same marks as an ordinary chart. Watching the frames change lets readers feel how often one outcome beats another instead of decoding an interval.
charts.anatomy: An ordinary chart whose marks jump between sampled outcomes several times a second, an optional frame counter, a caption saying each frame is one draw.
fits: Lay readers judging how reliable a difference is
Uncertainty in orderings, trends or other joint outcomes
Interactive media where animation is available
Building intuition that estimates could have been otherwise
limits: Needs animation; unusable in print or static reports
Readers cannot compare frames no longer on screen
Probabilities are estimated by watching, hence slow and imprecise
Frame rate and number of draws change what is perceived
Motion draws attention away from everything else

ours.scalability: a handful of marks per frame; 50+ draws at ~2–3 frames per second
ours.chart_types_md_section: Time series / Animation / bar chart race

charts.name: Difference view

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Gleicher et al. 2011

charts.summary: The difference between two states is computed and drawn as its own mark: diverging bars or a diverging heatmap of B minus A around a zero line, often placed next to the two originals. The reader sees the change directly instead of subtracting by eye.
charts.anatomy: A zero reference line or neutral colour, marks for B minus A in two directions, sorted items, optional side panels with the original values.
fits: Before versus after, plan versus actual, model versus observed
Small changes that side-by-side charts would hide
Ranking items by how much they changed
Matrices compared cell by cell
limits: Hides the absolute level unless the originals stay visible
Absolute and relative change tell different stories; name the one used
Only compares two states at a time
Differences of noisy values need their own uncertainty

ours.scalability: dozens of items as bars; hundreds × hundreds of cells as a heatmap

charts.name: Overview + detail

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Cockburn, Karlson & Bederson 2009 / Munzner 2014

charts.summary: Two linked views of one dataset: a small overview of everything and a larger detail view of the range the reader brushes in the overview. The detail may use another idiom. The overview keeps the reader oriented while they zoom.
charts.anatomy: A compact overview with a draggable selection rectangle, a larger detail view bound to that selection, shared scale direction, the selected extent shown in text.
fits: Long time series where local shape matters
Large scatterplots or maps explored region by region
Readers who must zoom without losing their place
Detail in a different idiom, such as a table of selected items
limits: Requires interaction; a static export shows only one selection
The reader must mentally connect two separate views
A selection that drives nothing is a broken promise
Costs screen space that a single chart would not
The default selection must already answer the main question

ours.scalability: tens of thousands of points in the overview; detail window as small as needed

charts.name: Arrow map

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from common cartographic practice (change-vector arrows per region); marks and channels after Munzner 2014

charts.summary: One arrow per region, anchored at the region, pointing in the direction of change between two periods and as long as the change is large. A glance shows where the shift went one way or the other and where it was strongest.
charts.anatomy: A plain base map, one arrow per region with a common origin rule, direction or colour for the sign of change, a legend showing a reference arrow length and direction.
fits: Change between exactly two periods across many regions
Showing direction and size of a shift together
Spatial patterns of gain versus loss
Results that swing between two options
limits: Arrows overlap where regions are small and dense
Shows change only; the level before or after is lost
Direction mapping is arbitrary and needs a legend
Long arrows reach into neighbouring regions
Unusable for more than two periods

ours.scalability: hundreds of regions; thin out in dense areas
ours.chart_types_md_section: Geospatial / Flow / line maps, network maps

charts.name: Spike map

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from common cartographic practice (spikes as a length-encoded symbol map); channel ranking after Munzner 2014

charts.summary: A thin vertical spike rises from each location with a height proportional to its value. Length is judged more accurately than circle area or colour, large regions get no extra weight, and spikes cover far less of the map than bubbles.
charts.anatomy: A muted base map, a narrow triangle or line anchored at each location, a height legend with reference values, taller spikes drawn over shorter ones.
fits: Totals per place, where a choropleth would mislead
Dense cities next to empty regions
Counts that span several orders of magnitude
Keeping the base map visible under the symbols
limits: Tall spikes cross their neighbours and seem to belong elsewhere
Heights are compared without a common baseline
Looks three-dimensional although it is not
Needs a height legend; values are not readable otherwise
Short spikes vanish beside very tall ones

ours.scalability: hundreds to a few thousand locations

charts.name: Tile cartogram

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Wilke 2019 / Munzner 2014

charts.summary: Every region becomes a tile of identical size, a square or hexagon, arranged to echo the real geography. Each unit receives the same ink, so small but populous regions are no longer drowned out by large empty ones, and tiles can hold a colour, a label or a tiny chart.
charts.anatomy: A grid of equal tiles in rough geographic position, a short code on each tile, colour for the value, a classed legend.
fits: Regions that count equally, such as seats or states
Maps where small regions vanish at true scale
Placing a mini chart per region in a geographic layout
Needs only a tile layout table, not region outlines
limits: True shapes, sizes and distances are gone
Neighbours on the grid are not always neighbours in reality
Readers must already know roughly where regions lie
No standard layout exists for most territories
Equal tiles misstate anything tied to land area

charts.name: Streamline map

source.note: Not in datavizcatalogue.com; added from Munzner 2014 / Ware 2013 / Laidlaw et al. 2005

charts.summary: A vector field such as wind or ocean current drawn over a map as curves that follow the local direction, or as a grid of small arrows. Speed goes to colour, stroke weight or, in animated versions, the pace of moving particles, where motion itself encodes the data.
charts.anatomy: A base map, streamlines or arrow glyphs tangent to the flow, arrowheads or fading tails for direction, a speed legend.
fits: Wind, currents or other continuous directional fields
Finding vortices, fronts and converging zones
Public weather graphics, animated
Showing direction and speed together
limits: Seeding density decides which features appear
Arrow grids clutter and alias with the sampling grid
Speed is read only roughly from colour or motion
A static frame hides how the field changes over time
Not for flows between discrete places

ours.scalability: any grid size; seed density tuned to the display
